By North Forty News Staff | NorthFortyNews.com

Researchers at Colorado State University are developing an artificial intelligence-powered forecasting system that could give Northern Colorado communities significantly more time to prepare for destructive hailstorms.

The National Science Foundation-funded project combines advanced radar technology, machine learning, and historical weather data to improve predictions of when and where damaging hail may strike.

For homeowners, farmers and businesses across the Front Range, the research could eventually mean the difference between having minutes to react and having hours—or even days—to prepare.

Traditional hail forecasting often provides only 30 to 60 minutes of warning. CSU researchers hope to extend that window by combining two different artificial intelligence systems.

One system, developed through a collaboration with NVIDIA, focuses on predicting how storms will develop over the next two to three hours. Another CSU model evaluates atmospheric conditions to estimate severe weather risks up to eight days ahead.

“We are working with AI to combine regional data from our radar systems with nine years of historic weather observations from across the whole U.S. to make a new forecasting tool,” said Kristen Rasmussen, an associate professor of atmospheric science at CSU.

Rasmussen emphasized that the technology remains under development, but CSU’s extensive experience with radar and severe weather research provides a strong foundation.

Colorado is among the nation’s most hail-prone states, with storms regularly causing extensive damage to roofs, vehicles, agricultural operations, and commercial properties.

Hail damage has also become a major contributor to rising homeowners insurance premiums statewide.

Researchers say the timing and intensity of damaging storms are changing, creating additional challenges for forecasters and insurers.
